title: Karpathy called it in 2023: "The hottest new programming language is…
body:
Karpathy called it in 2023: "The hottest new programming language is English."

Three years later, I feel it every single day.

I started my career writing Java.

Today most of my build time is spent writing English.

> System prompts.
> Specs.
> Instructions for agents.

Here's what surprised me.

My English is getting better. Not fancier. It's getting clearer.

Vague words give vague output.

Precise words give working software.

The edge isn't knowing more syntax anymore.

It's knowing exactly what you want and saying it plainly.

Is AI making you a better writer too?

title: Anthropic just launched Claude Duet.
body:
Anthropic just launched Claude Duet.

Claude waited for you to type. Duet doesn't wait.

It watches the apps you connect, briefs you every morning on what needs you, and gets work done while you are away. When it needs a decision, it messages you. Before anything risky like sending a message, paying someone or deleting something, it asks.

Research preview, waitlist only, US Pro and Max users for now. Runs on Opus 5.5. No extra cost, it uses your existing plan limits.

My take is, the chat box was never the destination. The shift is from AI you go to, to AI that comes to you, holding context on your work and your life.

Every assistant is heading there.

Anthropic just shipped a first version.

Link in comments.

title: 4 gates every PR passes through.
body:
4 gates every PR passes through. We've only automated 2.

 Gate 1. Does the code work.
 Gate 2. Is the code clean.
 Gate 3. Will it break in production.
 Gate 4. Will it spike the bill, cloud or model.

All good, merge. Not all good, don't merge.

Gates 1 and 2 are solved. Like this:

> CI runs the tests.
> Linters and now LLM reviewers handle the second one, and honestly they do it better than most of us humans do. Especially if it's 5pm on a Friday. :-)

Gates 3 and 4 are where it falls apart. Like this:

> The standard answer is load testing and staging.
> I've built those environments for a few teams and I'll say the quiet part: they run after the merge, on a schedule, against data that doesn't look like production. By the time they flag something, the commit is buried under 40 others and nobody can point at the one that did it.

So....

Gate 3 becomes an incident!

Gate 4 becomes a finance meeting in month 2!

That was survivable when a team shipped 15 PRs a week.

At 100s of PRs a week, with a lot of them model-authored, it isn't survivable.

The gate didn't get weaker.

The volume went up and the gate stayed exactly where it was.

What gates 3 and 4 actually need is the same shape as gates 1 and 2.

> Automatic.
> On the diff.
> Blocking. Before the merge, not after.

Nobody would ship without CI.

We ship without this every day.

I've spent a while now convinced that's the wrong tradeoff, and I've stopped just complaining about it.

title: The handoff is where multi agent systems die
body:
★ The handoff is where multi agent systems die ★

Multi agent systems fail in a very specific place, and it is not where people look.

They do not fail inside an agent.

Agent A does its job well.

Agent B does its job well.

The failure is in the handoff between them.

The baton drop in the middle.

Everyone romanticizes agent swarms right now.

More agents, more autonomy, elegant diagrams full of boxes and arrows.

Here is the part the diagram hides: every arrow between two boxes is a place where context can get mangled.

More agents means more handoffs means more silent failure points.

Complexity is not a feature.

Every agent you add is a new thing that can lie to the next one.

The hardest question in multi agent design is this: when the final output is wrong, which agent caused it?

Without scoring the handoffs, the honest answer is "no idea, restart the whole thing."

That is not engineering.

That is superstition with a compute bill.

And there is a subtle trap in how agents hand off.

If they pass context in natural language, they are playing telephone.

Small distortions compound down the chain.

By the fourth agent, the original intent is gone, and no single agent did anything obviously wrong.

The industry got very good at tracing what happened between agents.

Tracing shows you the path.

It does not tell you if the path was any good.

Those are different jobs.

Grading the handoff is the one that is still missing, and it is the one that matters for anything with money or compliance on the line.

My rule: a single agent that works beats a 5 agent architecture that looks impressive on a slide.

Add agents when one genuinely cannot do the job.

Not because orchestration looks smart.

If you run multi agent systems in production, where do yours actually break?

title: I've built 3 products in six years.
body:
I've built 3 products in six years.

It took me until this year to notice they were all the same company.

A synthetic monitoring platform that existed because enterprises refused to take their own dashboards at their word.

We verified from the outside, like a real user.

A prayer app where the AI is never allowed to play the oracle.

It listens, then routes to Scripture. The trusted source gives the answer. The software is the servant, never the source.

An open-source framework that grades AI agents on the path they took, not just the final answer, and refuses to emit a score without an explanation.

- Monitoring for infrastructure.
- Reverence for the sacred.
- Evals for agents.

One thesis underneath all of it. Don't ask people to trust you, hand them a way to verify.

I think that thesis is about to become the whole game.

When generating a convincing anything costs nothing, proof is the only currency that doesn't inflate.

I wrote the full argument, including my prediction for where the next decade of value goes.

Full article in the comments.

title: A valuable learning building PerfAgents: sell the sleep, not the…
body:
★ A valuable learning building PerfAgents: sell the sleep, not the software ★

I bootstrapped my last company to real ARR with a team of 20 and zero outside funding. Here is the single most useful thing I learned about enterprise.

Enterprise does not buy features. The champion and the teams at these enterprises buy the 𝘢𝘣𝘪𝘭𝘪𝘵𝘺 𝘵𝘰 𝘴𝘭𝘦𝘦𝘱 at night.

We built synthetic monitoring. Deeply unglamorous.

Our whole job was watching whether other companies' software was up, and paging the right person the moment it was not.

One of our customers was a fintech whose components sat inside the checkout flow of major US retailers such as Nordstrom and Lululemon. So while you were on one of those sites, moving toward buying something, our nodes around the world were quietly running that same path over and over. Not pinging a homepage.

Walking the real sequence, hitting the real APIs, from Frankfurt, from Singapore, from Virginia, every few minutes.

When something broke, we woke up the engineer who owned it. Before a single customer noticed.

That was the entire product. Nobody's engineer wants to learn about the outage from a customer on social media.

Not once did a feature list close a deal. What closed deals was answering one question fast and convincingly: what happens when your thing breaks at 3 am.

That reframe changed how I sell everything. Nobody at a Fortune 500 wants a dashboard. They want to not get the call from their CEO asking why checkout is down. They want to not be the person who gets blamed. Sell to that, the fear and the relief, not the fan's excitement about your UI.

The person who loves your demo is rarely the person who signs. Find the one who gets blamed when things break. That is your buyer.

The unsexy truth about monitoring, and honestly about a lot of great products: the better you do your job, the less anyone notices you.

We were most successful precisely when we were invisible.

Some of the best software is the thing nobody ever has to think about.

Founders, what is the "sleep at night" version of the thing you are selling?

Drop your comments.

title: When intelligence is free, meaning is the scarce thing
body:
34 startups raised over $200M this year.

Robot brains.

World models.

Chips.

Coding agents.

Nuclear plants to feed the data centers.

Every dollar is chasing the same thing.

Cheaper, faster intelligence.

Almost nobody is funding the other half.

What a person actually does with that intelligence once it costs nothing.

That is my bet.

When intelligence is free, meaning is the scarce thing.

So I build at the application layer, not the engine room.

ThyWord, my voice first prayer app, has 12,000 downloads and not one of those 34 is competing for the ground I am on.

Everyone is building the engine.

What we point it at is wide open.

title: Some prayers are not meant to be loud.
body:
Some prayers are not meant to be loud.

The ones whispered at 2am. The ones you say with your eyes closed in a crowded room. The ones too fragile to speak above a breath.

When we built ThyWord, we kept coming back to this. A prayer companion that only works when you raise your voice would miss the most honest moments of all.

So we tuned it for the quiet. You can whisper, barely move your lips, and ThyWord still catches your words and matches them to Scripture in real time.

This was not simple on the engineering side. Soft speech, low volume, breathy input. These are some of the hardest things to get right in voice. We spent real time on it, because the whisper is where so much of faith actually lives.

My grandmother prayed under her breath every morning. I never once heard the words clearly. But I always knew she was praying.

That is who we built this for.

Try it for yourself. Whisper a prayer and watch the Scripture come back to you.

Download ThyWord at thywordapp.com and tell me what you feel.

title: I build with AI every day.
body:
I build with AI every day.

Voice models, language models, pipelines that move faster than I can think.

And the more I build, the clearer one thing becomes.

AI can do a lot. It still can't do the things that make us human.

It can write a sympathy note. It can't sit with you.

It can draft an apology. It can't actually be sorry.

It can simulate care. It can't choose to care.

The hard part of being human was never the words. It was the meaning behind them.

The real risk isn't that AI replaces us. It's that we forget what only we can do.

Build with it. Don't outsource yourself to it.

title: The most useful language to learn in 2026 might be your own.
body:
The most useful language to learn in 2026 might be your own.

It's no longer Python or JavaScript.

I watched the Missional AI fireside chat between Pat Gelsinger and Steele Billings of Gloo, and one idea stuck with me.

They called it the reversal of Babel.

For about 70 years, being productive with a computer meant learning its language.

Syntax, commands, structure.

We adapted to the machine. We learned to use the text interface.

Now that is flipping.

The machine is learning to understand us.

Plain speech. Intent.

The way we actually talk.

What moved me was not the technical side of that. It was the spiritual side. So much of faith already lives in spoken words. Prayer is voice. Confession is voice. The oldest forms of worship were never typed.

For the first time, technology can meet people in that natural register instead of asking them to translate themselves into something a screen understands.

I build in this space every day, so maybe I am biased. But I think the quiet story of this era is not that machines got smarter. It is that they finally got close enough to hear us.

Grateful to the Missional AI community for the conversation.

title: Andrew Chen's argument lands hard from where I sit.
body:
Andrew Chen's argument lands hard from where I sit. I'm building ThyWord from a Jacksonville office, and the policy conversations shaping our industry are happening in rooms I'll likely never be in. Florida and Jacksonville should care about that, because the founders being shaped by these rules are right here, at kitchen tables, on short runways.

Andrew's pitch is simple. Whether your state or city has startups is a choice.

If you want them, you have to make conditions conducive, and you have to actually talk to Little Tech, not just the big incumbents and the industries getting disrupted.

He offers an open door for any policymaker who wants to sit with 5 or 10 genuinely small startups and hear what they actually need.

The throughline is pretty clear. Little Tech is structurally absent from policy debates, and the people writing the rules are hearing a skewed picture of what the industry actually looks like.

title: I was thinking about the B2C graveyard today.
body:
I was thinking about the B2C graveyard today.

Most consumer apps don't die because they had a bad idea. They die because they lost the "vibe." And in 2026, the vibe is powered by AI agents.

We’ve officially entered the era of Intent-and-Generate.

The modern consumer doesn't want to browse your menu or click through your filters. They want to say, "Fix this for me," and have an agent do the heavy lifting.

But here’s the problem: Consumers are way less forgiving than Enterprise CEOs.

If a B2B tool glitches, you open a Jira ticket.

If a B2C agent glitches. You know what happens next? That customer is gone. Forever. Delete. 1-star review.

This is why B2C needs deep Observability even more than the Enterprise guys do.

In the B2C world, "uptime" isn't enough anymore. You need to see the "why."

Why did the agent give that specific response?

Where exactly did the reasoning chain break?

Was it a slow API, or did the model just lose the plot?

If you can't trace that interaction in real-time, you aren't running a business; you’re running a lottery.

I’ve realized during my morning runs that you can't improve what you can't measure.

You can't fix your form if you don't know where you're over-striding.

B2C is exactly the same. If you aren't using something like an OTel-native stack to watch your agents, you're just running blind and hoping you don't hit a wall.

The "Prime Sport" of the future isn't just about who builds the smartest agent. It’s about who has the best eyes on the ground.

So, for the B2C founders out there:

How are you actually watching your agents?

Are you still "praying" it works, or have you moved to a real Observability stack?

Drop your preferred setup in the comments.

I'm curious if anyone is actually making legacy logs work for this, or if we’ve all finally moved on.

title: Anthropic Claude Opus 4.7 is here.
body:
Anthropic Claude Opus 4.7 is here.

The headline is coding, and rightly so.

Replit, Cursor, Factory, Notion, Vercel, Databricks, all reporting double digit lifts on the hardest tasks.

But the line that caught my eye sits further down the page: "more than three times" the image resolution of prior Claude models, and a new xhigh effort level for long, careful reasoning.

At ThyWord we care about a different flavor of hard.

A person whispers a prayer.

ThyWord hears them, understand what they are actually carrying, and match them to Scripture that meets them where they are. And then discards the original prayer.

When we do the matching, it's not the verse that sounds closest. The verse that fits, with the emotional weight.

That is a multimodal, long context, high stakes retrieval problem dressed up as a consumer app.

Every improvement in instruction following, honesty about limits, and sustained reasoning shows up directly in whether a young mom at 2am, with a baby who will not sleep and a mind that will not quiet, feels heard or feels like she talked to a chatbot.

Congrats to the Anthropic team. Excited to put 4.7 through its paces this week.

title: The era of the Chatbot is dead.
body:
The era of the Chatbot is dead.

We’ve moved from tools that talk to agents that execute.

In the Enterprise world, this isn't a productivity hack.

It’s a total architectural collapse of the old way.

Hiring interns to summarize PDFs is an old story now. The new story is, deploying coding agents to rewrite legacy pipelines while the C-suite sleeps.

But here’s the disruptive truth: The barrier to entry has vanished, and safety net went with it.

1. The Death of the "How"

In the consumer world, we used to pay for the "How". The coding, the design, the manual labor. With coding agents, the "How" is a commodity.

The distance between an idea and a shipped product is now measured in minutes. But speed without sight is just a faster way to hit a wall.

2. The Observability Mandate

If an agent is writing code, deploying microservices, and shifting data in real-time, you can't rely on old-school logs. Observability is the only heartbeat that matters.

You cannot secure what you cannot see.

You cannot trust what you cannot trace.

In a world of autonomous agents, deep observability is the only thing keeping your Enterprise from spinning into a black hole of unfixable technical debt.

3. Vulnerability vs. Acceptability

As agents start writing the world's infrastructure, the Vulnerability Side becomes the new frontline.

If an agent can build a feature in seconds, a bad actor’s agent can find a hole in milliseconds. We are entering the "Acceptability Phase", where the market only accepts AI-driven decisions if they are fully transparent and traceable.

What does this mean to Enterprises:

Coding agents have leveled the playing field, but they’ve also weaponized complexity.

The "Big Guys" are vulnerable to agile disruptors, and the "Agile Disruptors" are vulnerable to their own lack of oversight.

I think about this during my morning runs.

At mile 5, the noise drops away and you see the path for what it really is.

In tech, that clarity is everything. That clarity is called Observability.

If you aren't obsessing over how to watch your agents today, you won't have an Enterprise to run tomorrow. Period.

What kind of Observability stack do you prefer in the modern AI era?

Does OpenTelemetry cut it, or do we need something deeper?

Please comment below.

title: Everyone is talking about AI agents writing code.
body:
Everyone is talking about AI agents writing code.

Nobody is talking about who watches the code after it ships.

Anthropic just launched Managed Agents, Routines, and a full desktop experience for Claude Code.

This is not incremental.

They are building an operating system for the entire software engineering loop.

AI agents are about to deploy more code, more often, with less human review than anything we have seen before.

And the humans who used to catch problems by reading diffs and reviewing PRs?

They will be outnumbered.

When a human writes bad code, another human usually catches it in review.

When an AI agent writes bad code and ships it at 2am through an automated pipeline, the only thing standing between you and an outage is your observability stack.

Observability is no longer a monitoring tool. It is the immune system of software.

The next era belongs to platforms that move from "here is a dashboard showing something broke" to "we detected the anomaly, identified the root cause, and rolled it back before your customers noticed."

Agents watching agents. Built natively on open standards like OpenTelemetry.

Transparent pricing. Autonomous operations.

I have spent almost two decades helping enterprises adopt complex infrastructure.

The pattern is always the same: the picks and shovels win.

In the AI agent era, observability is the picks and shovels.

Would love to hear what my fellow LinkedIn people think about it?

title: Anthropic unveiled Mythos exactly a week ago on Tuesday, April 7, 2026.
body:
Anthropic unveiled Mythos exactly a week ago on Tuesday, April 7, 2026.

It finds zero-day vulnerabilities in every major operating system.

It chains 4 bugs into a working browser exploit overnight.

It reverse engineers closed source binaries.

Engineers with no security background are waking up to finished exploits in their inbox.

If you work in observability, read that again.

For 24 years we have built stacks that assume the attacker moves at human speed.

Dashboards refresh every minute.

Alerts fire on thresholds tuned for last quarter's traffic.

Incident response runbooks assume a person is reading logs, forming a hypothesis, opening a ticket.

THAT ENTIRE MENTAL MODEL JUST GOT OBSOLETE.

When an AI can discover and weaponize a 27 year old bug in OpenBSD in a single run, your mean time to detect (MTTD) is no longer measured in minutes.

It is measured in how fast your telemetry pipeline can reason.

Logs, metrics and traces are not enough anymore.

You need SEMANTIC OBSERVABILITY.

Systems that understand what the data means, not just what it says.

A few things I am watching closely.

Synthetic monitoring is going to get reborn.

Not as scripted Selenium flows, but as adversarial agents probing your own surface the way Mythos would.

If you are not red teaming your production with AI, someone else is.

OpenTelemetry becomes the substrate.

The winners in this next wave are the platforms that can ingest everything and let a model reason across it in real time.

Dash0 is making that bet natively on OpenTelemetry.

Chronosphere is making it from the cloud native scale angle.

Both are reading the room correctly.

The legacy three pillar vendors are not.

The SOC and the SRE merge.

You cannot separate reliability from security when the same model can both find the bug and trigger the outage.

One pane of glass is no longer a vendor slogan.

It is survival.

I spent years building synthetic monitoring at PerfAgents and watching enterprise teams drown in signal without meaning.

Mythos does not create that problem.

It exposes how unprepared we already were.

The observability category is about to get rewritten.

The tools that survive will be the ones that think, not just the ones that store.

Who else is thinking about this? I want to compare notes.

title: "Wow, whoever has made this app..."

title: Everyone is building AI that talks like God.
body:
Everyone is building AI that talks like God.

We built something that listens like your grandmother.

That line is the headline of a story about ThyWord that ran on MarketWatch this week. Still feels strange to type that sentence.

Six weeks ago we launched a voice first prayer companion on iOS and Android. The idea was simple. Most prayer apps tell you what to say. We wanted one that actually hears you, then meets you in Scripture. No scripts. No performance. The kind of presence my grandmother had. She would close her eyes and pray for me out loud.

I did not expect a financial news site to be the one that picked up the story. But maybe that is the point. The Meaning Economy is real. As AI gets louder and faster, people are quietly looking for something slower and deeper. Six days a week between Sundays, most of us are figuring out faith on our own. ThyWord is for those six days.

Building this has been the most meaningful work of my career. It also sits alongside two decades of enterprise architecture, observability, and platform work that I am still very much in love with. Two tracks, one operator.

If you want to read the piece, it is on MarketWatch under the headline above.

And if you want to try the app, it is called ThyWord on the App Store and Google Play.

title: The Tomb is a Prerequisite, Not a Failure!
body:
The Tomb is a Prerequisite, Not a Failure!

Three words have reshaped history for over 2,000 years: He is risen.

They've endured not because of a distribution strategy or perfect branding.

They've endured because they speak to a fundamental truth about the human condition.

As a founder, I've been thinking a lot about the Easter story this year. When you build a startup, you live inside a cycle that strangely mirrors this narrative.

You pour your life into something you believe in, only to watch it get crushed by the market, by doubt, or by metrics that refuse to cooperate.

Every founder I know has had their "Friday."

The day the bank account hits zero.

The day the lead investor says no.

The day you sit in your driveway, wondering if you're actually just crazy.

In tech, we worship iteration.

We celebrate the "pivot." But we rarely talk about the deeper engine underneath it all: Hope.

Optimism says, "Things will probably work out." Hope says, "Even if they don't, there is something worth building that outlasts the outcome."

I started ThyWord because I believe we are entering the Meaning Economy.

AI is automating knowledge, tasks, and workflows. But it will never automate meaning.

It cannot replicate the moment a mother whispers a prayer over her child at 2 AM, or the way a piece of Scripture meets you exactly where you are in a moment of despair.

Technology is just the tool. Purpose is the operating system.

In the startup world, we call it a "breakthrough" or a "comeback." In my faith, we call it Sunday.

Whether you're a founder grinding through your Friday, an engineer building in the dark, or a leader carrying a team through uncertainty, remember that the greatest comeback story ever told didn't need a slide deck.

Sunday is coming.

title: Friday is good.
body:
Friday is good.

Not because the week is over.
Not because the weekend is here.

Friday is good because sometimes the worst day becomes the most important one.

Every founder knows this feeling.

The day your biggest customer churns. The day your co-founder says "we need to talk." The day your bank account hits a number that makes your stomach drop.

You don't call those days good while you're in them. You call them good later. When you realize that was the day everything actually changed.

Two thousand years ago, a Friday looked like complete failure. A movement was over. The leader was gone. His closest team abandoned the project.

Nobody standing there called it good.

But that Friday became the most consequential product launch in human history. Three days later, everything changed. And we still talk about it.

So if you're in your "Friday" right now, the fundraise fell through, the product broke, the deal died, just know this:

Some Fridays only look bad from the inside.

Have a blessed Good Friday. The story isn't over.

Repost if your worst day turned into your best chapter.

title: My grandmother prayed every single day of her life.
body:
My grandmother prayed every single day of her life.

She told our family that at least one person should spend time in God's presence every day. I carried that with me across continents, career changes, and decades in tech. But I could never live up to it. Not consistently. Not with four kids and a demanding career.

So I built something.

ThyWord is a voice first prayer companion. You pray out loud. The app listens and responds with a Scripture that speaks to what you're feeling.

No chatbot. No celebrity. No AI pretending to be God.

Since launching on Ash Wednesday, more than 2,500 prayers have been spoken into the app by over 1,250 people.

And, every second a prayer is being done on ThyWord. That's incredible and honestly I never thought that it would happen so soon as this.

Gratitude is the most common emotion. Then Spiritual Growth. Then Healing. Then Strength.

This Easter, while the largest faith apps spend millions on Super Bowl ads and celebrity partnerships, we're proving something simpler: people just want to pray and be heard.

I call it the six days between Sundays problem. You leave church feeling connected. By Monday, the noise takes over. By Friday, the connection is gone. ThyWord exists for the Tuesday afternoon, not the Sunday morning.

title: Two data exposures at Anthropic in under a week.
body:
Two data exposures at Anthropic in under a week.

And both of them trace back to the same root cause: gaps in OPERATIONAL discipline.

First, nearly 3,000 unpublished assets left in a publicly searchable CMS because the default setting was public and nobody enforced a policy to change it.

Then days later, a source map file ships with a routine Claude Code npm update, exposing 500,000+ lines of source code. A known Bun bug had been open for 20 days. Nobody caught it before it hit production.

No customer data was compromised. But this is exactly why DevOps matters.

Build pipeline hygiene.

Environment configuration audits.

Automated checks that catch what humans miss before it ever leaves the gate.

Default settings that are secure by design, not by hope. These aren't nice to haves. They're the guardrails that keep your entire operation from becoming a headline.

If your CI/CD pipeline doesn't have a gate that flags debug artifacts, misconfigured defaults, or known upstream bugs before deployment, you're one npm publish away from the same story.

Shipping fast is great.

Shipping safely is the job.

More detailed breakdown coming soon. Stay tuned.

title: In late 2024, I took a demo from Dash0 when they were a small team with…

title: Most apps ask you to type.
body:
Most apps ask you to type. We ask you to speak.

When we built ThyWord, we made a deliberate design choice: voice first, everything else second.

No keyboard. No scrolling through menus.

You open the app, tap one button, and start talking.

Why?

Because prayer isn't something you type. It's something you pour out.

And when someone is in a moment of need, the last thing they want is friction.

Behind that simple microphone button is a real time speech to Scripture matching engine.

You speak what's on your heart, and ThyWord listens and responds with the exact Bible verses that speak to your situation.

title: I've been building in public for a few weeks now and here's my hottest…
body:
I've been building in public for a few weeks now and here's my hottest take so far:

The keyboard is a bottleneck for the soul.

Let me explain.

When I started building ThyWord, our voice first prayer companion app, I assumed the hard part would be the AI. Getting the speech recognition right. Matching prayers to Scripture accurately.

And yeah, that stuff is hard.

But the real unlock wasn't technical. It was emotional.

When someone speaks a prayer out loud, they're not editing themselves. They're not backspacing. They're not crafting the perfect sentence. They're just... being honest.

And that honesty is data that text based AI will never fully capture.

Voice carries tone. Pace. Pauses. The crack in someone's voice when they're asking for help. None of that comes through in a text box.

This is why I believe voice is the most underrated frontier in AI right now.

Not voice assistants that set timers. Not voice clones that mimic celebrities.

I'm talking about AI that actually listens to the meaning behind someone's words.

We're building this at ThyWord and sharing the journey openly because I think more founders need to explore this space. The technology is ready. The models are good enough. What's missing is imagination.

Voice isn't just an input method. It's the most human way we have to connect.

And AI should meet us there.

title: Most AI companies are obsessed with text.
body:
Most AI companies are obsessed with text.

Chatbots. Prompts. Typing into a box.

But here's what I think everyone is sleeping on: the future of AI isn't typed. It's spoken.

Think about it. We don't naturally communicate by typing. We talk. We speak out. We whisper. We pray.

Voice is the oldest interface humans have. And yet most of the AI world is still building for screens and keyboards.

I'm building ThyWord, a voice first prayer app that listens to your spoken prayers and responds with Scripture in real time. And what I've learned building this in public over the last few months is something that surprised me.

People don't want to type their deepest thoughts. They want to say them out loud.

There's something that happens when you speak a prayer versus when you type one. It hits different. It's more raw. More real. The voice carries weight that text simply cannot.

And when AI can meet someone in that moment, not with a chatbot response but with the right Scripture at the right time, that's when technology stops feeling like technology.

We're in the early innings of voice AI. Not just for prayer, but for therapy, for journaling, for coaching, for gratitude.

The companies that figure out how to build AI that truly listens (not just transcribes) are going to change how people interact with technology forever.

I'm betting my company on it.

If you're also building at the intersection of voice and AI, I'd love to connect. This space is wide open and I think the best is still ahead.

title: A person full of pride is always angry.
body:
A person full of pride is always angry.

We easily get upset when things don't go our way.

You work late nights on a project but your manager barely notices.

You give it everything and it still feels like it wasn't enough.

That constant frustration?

It often comes from pride.

The hidden belief that we must be perfect and in total control.

When we stop trying to be the smartest person in the room, we drop a heavy burden.

You don't have to be flawless to earn your seat at the table.

Next time frustration tries to steal your peace, try these simple steps:

1. Pause and breathe. When the pressure makes your temper rise, step away for a moment. Give yourself space to think clearly instead of reacting.

2. Accept setbacks. A lost deal, a missed promotion. These are not signs of failure. They're part of the journey.

3. Rest and step back. Your worth is not tied to your last performance review. You are more than your title or your LinkedIn headline.

Peace comes from having the humility to admit we don't have all the answers. And that's not weakness.

That's wisdom.

Whether you pray, meditate, journal, or just sit in silence, find that thing that brings you back to the center.

The grind never stops. But you're allowed to.

What helps you find peace when frustration hits?

Drop it in the comments.

title: What really happened to the world's most loved AI Dev Tool, Cursor AI…

AI still requires coding, configurations and right placement and orchestration and a human in between.

Let's dive into what happened with Cursor AI.

Cursor AI lost customers overnight due to a situation where its AI-powered support bot hallucinated a policy change, falsely stating that users were not allowed to log in from multiple machines. This misinformation, coupled with actual technical issues causing users to get logged out when switching devices, led to mass cancellations and a significant erosion of user trust.

What works best is a 50:50 approach.

Half Human & Half AI.

title: The problem of invisibility!
body:
The problem of invisibility!

Date: July 19, 2024.

It appeared to be a typical day.

Hustlers were hustling, and bustling environments worldwide were bustling with activities. Daily life seemed perfect and normal. But something catastrophic was going to happen across the world.

The world was about to witness "the largest" global IT outage in human history.

What seemed to be a regular patch update turned out as "the most faulty" update and invited the "blue screen of death," impacting 8.5 million Microsoft Windows devices.

Digital public infrastructure crumbled!

Businesses, industries, and governments were disrupted!

Thousands of flights were grounded!

Critical surgeries were postponed!

And users of specific banking platforms faced difficulties accessing their accounts!

What caused all of these?

CrowdStrike, a renowned security software company, protected these devices.

CrowdStrike runs "Falcon," a software agent that operates at "ring 0" or kernel level of the OS for end-point detection and prevention. An update to this agent was rolled out with "no regression tests". There was no visibility to the problem, and there was no visibility to the impact in the beginning.

The result of the outage was catastrophic.

It proved one thing - "Software runs the world."

And it underlines one crucial thing in "testing" and "monitoring" space.

No matter how great your code is and your software product is, if your software is not tested in the way the end users use it, there is no guarantee that it will work the way it should. Visibility to the availability of the software is as important as the existence of the software itself.

That is the reason, Observability is a key area businesses worldwide should really focus on.

No matter whether the business is small or large, the emphasis on proper testing and monitoring is crucial. And visibility to the software system to see that it works fine from user locations is more relevent, even in this modern era of AI driven world.

Monitoring the availability of the software is so critical to save humankind from these kind of impactful outages.

Ensuring continuous monitoring will prevent such outages to a great extent.

If "availability monitoring" was in place, the range of disruption these software outages brought in could have been prevented or alleviated.

This is specifically relevant for SaaS and AI Agentic software.

This can happen to any software company and any software product. The only way to prevent such outages is to monitor for outages proactively and take action before they can have a widespread impact.

That's the story of visibility, the problem of invisibility.

For your SaaS offerings, use synthetic monitoring by mimicking critical browser flows using the Microsoft-backed open-source framework - Playwright.

To run these scripts on Amazon Web Services (AWS) worldwide, use PerfAgents. You don't have to live in the fear of unpredictability and invisibility.

title: Automating a user flow should be easy.
body:
Automating a user flow should be easy. Playwright is one of the best frameworks to do web automation.

But once you write the web automation scripts using Playwright you need an infra to run these scripts. Even if you want to run it periodically, it is kind of a pain in the ***.

You can spin up a Kubernetes (Official) cluster to run this. And use GitHub Actions or Jenkins or something else to schedule it. Solves the problem a bit. But does this mean you should not do web automation? No, web automation is essential to test your user flows and is even more important to test it periodically from different regions around the world.

That's the reason, there are synthetic monitoring products exists.

Now, there are a few tools that do Playwright well, but I have not found a single tool that can be like a single pane of glass view for testing and monitoring like PerfAgents does. Please tag in the comments if there are good tools that can replace PerfAgents.

Our Team: Well, it preemptively identifies issues before they impact end users, much like the existing tools. However, the difference is that, with PerfAgents, you can monitor your software just as you use it. And that's how we stand out from the existing tools.

Early Adopter: Please tell me about the differentiation.
Our Team: For sure. While other tools focus on monitoring production as a stand-alone activity, PerfAgents focuses on reusing the same test cases you have written for testing to be used for continuous monitoring.

Early Adopter: Sounds interesting!
Our Team: Great. To ensure your software works well end-to-end for your end users from their location and browsers, you need to monitor your production system continuously from locations you anticipate your users will access from and from browsers you think your users will use.

Early Adopter: Agreed!
Our Team: The whole user flow you anticipate your user will perform can be scripted, pre-scripted, using a test credential or a test user.

Early Adopter: Nice. Is that what synthetic monitoring is?
Our Team: Yes, and the best way you do it is by employing end-to-end web automation practices.

Early Adopter: What language or platform can I use to do that?
Our Team: Traditional monitoring systems developed custom recorders to record end-to-end tests for monitoring purposes. However, the downside is that they can only sometimes be run against lower environments, and even if they could, they would accumulate cost and add effort. That's why an excellent open-source web automation framework is most beneficial for these scenarios. The TLDR is: Use a good web automation framework to do your job.

Early Adopter: What would be a good example?
Our Team: Playwright, an open-source tool developed by Microsoft, is the best web automation tool currently available. Other frameworks, such as Selenium, Cypress, and Pptr, can also be used for the same use cases.

Early Adopter: Great. What languages do they support?
Our Team: They support a wide variety of languages, including Javascript and Python. Pptr, however, is for NodeJS alone, and it's not growing as much as the rest of the tools.

Early Adopter: Great. So, if I understand correctly, PerfAgents will let me run my Playwright script as a synthetic monitoring script to capture my application's performance data and alert me if latency is detected or if there is an issue loading any web page or API. Am I correct in my understanding?
Our Team: Precisely.

Early Adopter: Great, let's talk about the next steps!
Our Team: Sure!

TLDR - Then, they come on board and live a happy life as a customer ever after.

title: Synthetics & Canary combined, can prevent 90% of world's software…
body:
Synthetics & Canary combined, can prevent 90% of world's software outages!

How?

With Synthetic Monitoring you can mimic users actions and can automate your end-to-end test cases.

Now run this in lower environments or the-so-called-qa-env to find issues early on.

Once you find that there are no net-new issues after running the synthetic tests for 48 hours (bare minimum), you are good to release the code to production.

Now, release using the canary method, so that you don't release it to the entire user set, but only a subset of your users.

This is the power combination of Synthetics+Canary and it can prevent 90 % of all outages happening across the web.

If you would like to catch a virtual coffee with me to discuss more, I'm only a few clicks away.

Here is my calendar - https://lnkd.in/eYFH5uPr

PS: Synthetic monitoring requires you to write synthetic tests, preferably written using Playwright or similar such frameworks. Canary deployment is a practice but there are tools such as Harness that have ready-to-go canary deployment processes.
